meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Tubman's in spirit — she never lost a passenger — but the polished wording can't be pinned to any primary source. Attributed, not verified.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: c. 1822 – 10 March 1913 · abolitionist & Underground Railroad conductor
answer.sourceLine: Widely and consistently credited to Tubman, and it squares with her documented record — she truly never lost a fugitive. But the exact wording appears in neither of her authorized biographies (Sarah Bradford’s 1869 life and its 1886 rewrite); its earliest documented print is a 1996 quotation anthology, so no primary source pins these words to her mouth.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Often tied to an 1896 women’s-suffrage convention — unverified

Absent from Bradford’s 1869 and 1886 authorized lives

source.excerpt: I was the conductor of the Underground Railroad for eight years, and I can say what most conductors can’t say — I never ran my train off the track, and I never lost a passenger.
trail: The line appears nowhere in Sarah Bradford’s Scenes in the Life of Harriet Tubman (1869) — Tubman’s first authorized biography — nor in the 1886 rewrite Harriet, the Moses of Her People.
What the 1869 book does record is the fact underneath the boast: Thomas Garrett’s letter attests that “no slave who placed himself under her care, was ever arrested that I have heard of” (p. 50).
Wikiquote files the line in its general Quotes section, sourced only to a 1996 anthology — not to any 19th-century text.

Its notorious sibling — “I freed a thousand slaves…” — is branded “completely spurious” by specialists Jean Humez and Kate Clifford Larson (Wikiquote, Disputed); this railroad line has not been debunked, but it is equally unsourced to a primary.
source.excerptNote: The fuller form in which the line usually circulates. No 19th-century source records Tubman saying it; the wording is documented in print only from the late 20th century onward.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording cannot be tied to any datable primary work: it is absent from both of Tubman’s pre-1931 authorized biographies (1869, 1886) and surfaces in print only in modern quotation anthologies from the 1990s onward. Because the origin of the wording is unknown, no copyright status can be asserted — and it cannot be called public-domain on the strength of a specific old edition, since none contains it.

author.name: Harriet Tubman
author.kicker: The true record behind the line
author.heading: Harriet Tubman
author.bio: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and returned roughly thirteen times over the next decade to guide some seventy enslaved people north — earning the name “Moses.” She later served the Union Army as scout, spy and nurse, and spent her final decades in Auburn, New York, active in the women’s-suffrage movement. Her contemporaries confirmed the boast behind this quote: none of the fugitives in her charge was ever recaptured.

misattribution.heading: What’s really going on
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong person — the sentiment is genuinely Tubman’s and the boast is factually true. The problem is provenance: a polished, much-shared sentence presented as her documented words, yet traceable to no primary source.

items.why: The exact line is absent from both authorized biographies — Bradford’s 1869 and 1886 volumes — and its earliest documented appearance in print is a 1996 anthology (Wikiquote cites Women’s Words, p. 2).
Tubman did speak at the 1896 Rochester suffrage convention, but the records of that appearance (House Divided) contain no such line; the pairing of quote and occasion is a modern popular association.

A different Tubman-branded line that specialists Jean Humez and Kate Clifford Larson call “completely spurious” (first printed 1993, no earlier source) — see Wikiquote, Disputed. It is often quoted alongside the railroad line, blurring the two.

misattribution.truthLine: The record behind the boast is real: Tubman genuinely never lost a passenger — abolitionist Thomas Garrett swore no fugitive in her care was ever taken (Bradford, 1869, p. 50) — even if this particular sentence can’t be traced to her own mouth.

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: Tubman built her legend on a single railroad metaphor: she was “the conductor,” the freedom-seekers were her “passengers,” the safe houses were “stations.” A line that turns that metaphor into a clean, proud boast — never off the track, never a passenger lost — is almost too perfect not to quote.

And its power is that the boast is true. Across some thirteen missions Tubman brought roughly seventy people out of slavery, and by every contemporary account not one was recaptured on her watch. The sentence fails only the narrow test a provenance site must apply: no one can show where or when she actually said it.
context.pull: The boast is true even if the sentence is unsourced — she really never lost a passenger.
